content: In biology, the term axenic refers to a culture of a specific organism that is completely devoid of any other contaminating organisms. The earliest axenic cultures were developed for bacteria or unicellular eukaryotes, but it is also possible to create axenic cultures for various multicellular organisms. Axenic cultures are particularly valuable because all the organisms within them are genetically identical or share the same gene pool. This genetic uniformity ensures that the organisms respond in a consistent and reproducible manner, which simplifies the interpretation of experimental results. To prepare axenic cultures of microorganisms, a dilution series is typically employed using an existing mixed culture. The culture is progressively diluted to the point where subsamples contain only a few individual organisms, ideally just a single organism in the case of asexual species. These subsamples are then allowed to grow until the identity of the organisms within them can be determined. Only those cultures that consist of the desired type of organism are selected, resulting in an axenic culture. Subcultures derived from a single organism or cell without genetic alteration are classified as clones. Axenic cultures are routinely monitored to ensure they remain free of contamination. A common method for verifying the axenic status of a culture involves spreading a sample onto an agar plate and incubating it for a specified period. The agar used should be an enriched medium capable of supporting the growth of common contaminating organisms. If any contaminating organisms are present, they will grow on the plate during incubation, thereby identifying cultures that are no longer axenic.
